chapters.title: Chapter 1: Getting Started with Python
chapters.goal: Set up Copilot and AI tooling to build your first application and then learn the core concepts and syntax so you can understand it fully.

examples.title: Hello World
examples.description: Write a simple Hello World program in Python to get started.
examples.prompt: Write a Hello World app

explanation.summary: This one-line program displays the text "Hello, World!" on the screen. It is the traditional first program in any language, used to confirm that Python is installed and working.

lines.text: print is a built-in function that sends text to the screen. The words inside the quotation marks form a string, and the parentheses pass that string to print as the value to display.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Core Concepts
chapters.goal: Generate applications with prompts that use core Python concepts and learn how the code works with illustrated examples of Python core concepts.

examples.title: Basket of Fruits
examples.description: Create a program that manages a basket of fruits using variables and basic operations.
examples.prompt: Write a six line program with three baskets for apples, oranges, and bananas.

explanation.summary: This program stores a count of three kinds of fruit in three variables and then prints each count with a label. It is a first look at how a name in Python holds a value you can use later.

lines.text: The equals sign is an assignment: it creates a variable named apples and stores the number 5 in it. Nothing is displayed yet, the value is simply being remembered.
Each basket gets its own variable name, so the three counts stay separate and can be changed independently.
print can take several values separated by commas; it shows the text label "Apples:" followed by the number stored in the variable, with a space between them.
Notice that the quoted text is printed literally while the bare word bananas is looked up as a variable — that difference is the heart of this exercise.

examples.title: Add Three Numbers
examples.description: Create a program that adds three numbers and prints the result.
examples.prompt: Write a program that adds 3 numbers and prints the result
response: # Add three numbers and print the result
# You can change these numbers as needed

explanation.summary: This program stores three numbers in variables, adds them together, and prints the total. It shows the basic pattern of holding values in named variables and combining them with an operator.

lines.text: The name num1 is bound to the value 5, so the number can be referred to by name later instead of being repeated.
The three variables are added and the total is stored in result, keeping the calculation separate from the display of it.
Passing two arguments to print puts a label before the number, and print automatically separates them with a space.

print("The average weight of an apple and an orange is", average_weight, "pounds.")

explanation.summary: This program stores the typical weight of an apple and an orange as decimal numbers, then works out the average of the two and prints the result.

The second weight gets its own variable, which keeps the two measurements separate and makes the arithmetic below easy to read.

examples.title: Convert String to Uppercase
examples.description: Convert the string 'i lOvE pUpPiEs' to uppercase using Python's string methods.
examples.prompt: Convert the string "i lOvE pUpPiEs" to uppercase

explanation.summary: This program takes a string with mixed capitalization and prints it with every letter in uppercase, using Python's built-in string method upper().

lines.text: Stores the original string in a variable named text. The deliberately jumbled capitalization shows that upper() does not care what case the letters started in.

Calls the upper() method on the string, which returns a new all-capitals string. The original text is unchanged, because strings in Python cannot be modified in place; the result must be saved in a variable.
Displays the converted string so you can see the effect of the method call.

examples.title: Print Item Price
examples.description: Print the price of a specified item using an f-string and string concatenation.

prompts.prompt: Print the price of a specified item using an f string

explanation.summary: This program stores an item name and its price in variables, then builds a single sentence from them using an f-string. An f-string lets you drop variable values directly into text without stitching pieces together by hand.

lines.text: The name of the product is stored as a string, in quotation marks, so it can be reused in the message below.
The price is a float, Python's type for numbers with a decimal point, which is what money amounts need.

The f before the opening quote marks this as an f-string, so Python replaces {item} and {price} with the values of those variables. The dollar sign before {price} is ordinary text and is printed as-is, because only names inside braces get substituted.

prompts.prompt: Print the price of a specified item using string concatenation
response: print("The price of the " + item + " is $" + str(price))

explanation.summary: This program stores an item name and its price in variables, then builds one sentence out of them and prints it. It shows that a number must be converted to text before it can be joined to a string.

lines.text: The name of the item is stored as a string, in quotes, so it can be dropped into the sentence later.
The price is a float, a number with a decimal point, which Python treats as a number rather than text.

lines.code: print("The price of the " + item + " is $" + str(price))
lines.text: The + operator joins strings end to end, a process called concatenation. Because price is a number, str(price) converts it to text first; without that conversion Python would refuse to add a number to a string. Note the spaces inside the quotes, which keep the words from running together.

examples.title: Ask About the Weather
examples.description: Write and print a simple Boolean statement indicating if it is sunny today.
examples.prompt: Write a simple Boolean statement about the weather and print it

explanation.summary: This program stores a yes-or-no fact about the weather in a Boolean variable and prints it alongside a question. Booleans are Python's type for values that can only be True or False.

lines.text: True is a Boolean literal, not the text "True", so it must be capitalised exactly this way. Naming the variable is_sunny signals to a reader that it holds a yes-or-no answer.
Passing two values to print displays them both, separated by a space, so the question and its answer appear on one line.

examples.title: Name and Greeting
examples.description: Ask the user for their name and print a greeting.
examples.prompt: Ask for the user's name and print it

explanation.summary: This short program asks the reader to type their name, then greets them by name. It shows how to collect input from a person and place it inside a message.

lines.text: The input function displays the prompt text, waits for the user to type something and press Enter, and hands back whatever was typed as a string, which is stored in the variable name.
The f before the quotes makes this an f-string, so Python replaces {name} with the value the user entered instead of printing the word "name" literally.

examples.title: Pet Type and Name
examples.description: Ask for the type and name of the user's pet and output it.
examples.prompt: Ask for a pet's type and name, and output it
response: pet_type = input("What type of pet do you have? ")
pet_name = input("What is your pet's name? ")

explanation.summary: This program asks two questions at the keyboard and then combines both answers into one friendly sentence. It shows how several pieces of input can be gathered before anything is displayed.

lines.code: pet_type = input("What type of pet do you have? ")
lines.text: The text inside input() is the prompt shown to the reader, and whatever they type is stored in the variable pet_type. Note the space at the end of the prompt so the typed answer does not run into the question mark.

lines.code: pet_name = input("What is your pet's name? ")
lines.text: A second input() call collects the pet's name. Because the prompt is wrapped in double quotes, the apostrophe in "pet's" is treated as an ordinary character rather than closing the string.
The f before the quotes makes this an f-string, so each name in braces is replaced by the value stored in that variable when the line runs.

examples.title: Treat Calorie Calculator
examples.description: Get how many treats a dog ate, and how many calories are in each treat. Calculate calorie consumption.
examples.prompt: Get how many treats a dog ate, and how many calories are in each treat. Calculate calorie consumption.
response: # Get user input for number of treats and calories per treat
num_treats = int(input("How many treats did the dog eat? "))
calories_per_treat = float(input("How many calories are in each treat? "))

explanation.summary: This program asks how many treats a dog ate and how many calories each treat has, then multiplies the two to report the total calories consumed.

lines.code: num_treats = int(input("How many treats did the dog eat? "))
lines.text: Input always arrives as text, so int() converts the reply into a whole number that can be used in arithmetic. A count of treats is naturally a whole number, so int is the right choice here.

lines.code: calories_per_treat = float(input("How many calories are in each treat? "))
lines.text: Here float() is used instead of int() because calorie values often include a decimal part, such as 25.5.
Multiplying the count by the calories in one treat gives the total, and storing it in a name keeps the calculation separate from the printing.
The f before the quotes marks an f-string, which lets you drop a variable straight into the text inside curly braces.

examples.title: Data Types
examples.prompt: Write an eight line program to print attributes of a giraffe using basic data types.

explanation.summary: This program stores several facts about a giraffe in variables, each using one of Python's basic data types, then prints them all in a single formatted report.

lines.text: Text in quotes is a string, the type Python uses for names and any other sequence of characters.
A number written with a decimal point is a float, which is what you need for measurements that fall between whole numbers. The `_m` in the name is a reminder that the value is in metres.
A number with no decimal point is an integer, suitable for a weight recorded to the nearest kilogram.
`False` is a boolean, the type with only two possible values, `True` and `False`. Naming such a variable as a yes/no question makes the code read naturally.

The `f` before the quote makes this an f-string, so each name in curly braces is replaced by its variable's value. Each `\n` is a newline character, which is why one print call produces seven lines of output.

examples.title: Math
examples.prompt: Write a Python program that adds up the number of feet for a penguin, a panda, and a hippo.
response: # Define the number of feet for each animal

explanation.summary: This program stores the number of feet each of three animals has, adds them together, and prints each count along with the total.

lines.text: A variable name that says what the number means keeps the arithmetic below readable; a bare 2 would tell you nothing.
Adding the variables rather than the literal numbers means the total stays correct if you change any animal's count above.
The f before the quotes marks this as an f-string, so Python replaces {penguin_feet} with the variable's value instead of printing the name.
Printing the sum last gives the reader the individual counts first, so they can check the arithmetic themselves.

examples.title: Pet Fetch
examples.prompt: Write a 5 line program to calculate the number of balls thrown. Take user input for the number of balls the dog retrieved, the number of balls the cat retrieved, and the number of balls that never got retrieved.
response: Enter number of balls dog retrieved: 8
Enter number of balls cat retrieved: 2
Enter number of balls never retrieved: 3

explanation.summary: This program asks for three counts — balls the dog brought back, balls the cat brought back, and balls that were never retrieved — and adds them together to report how many balls were thrown in total. What the book shows is a sample run: the numbers after each colon are what the reader typed in.

lines.code: Enter number of balls dog retrieved: 8
lines.text: The text up to the colon is the prompt the program displays; the 8 is typed by the person running it and is read in as a string, so it must be converted with int() before it can be added.

lines.code: Enter number of balls cat retrieved: 2
lines.text: A second input call collects the cat's tally, stored in its own variable so the three counts stay separate.

lines.code: Enter number of balls never retrieved: 3
lines.text: Balls that were thrown but never came back still count toward the total, which is why this third number is collected.
The three numbers are summed with + and printed; because they were converted to integers, 8 + 2 + 3 gives 13 rather than the joined text "823".

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Loops and Flow Control
chapters.goal: Build applications with more complex logic using Python control structures.

examples.title: Temperature Hat Check
examples.description: This code asks the user the temperature, then uses an if statement to determine whether they need a hat. The program is then modified to include an else statement that tells you when you don't need a hat, and finally an elif conditional for sunscreen when it's too hot.

prompts.prompt: Write a 3 line program that tells you to wear a hat if the temperature is too low.

explanation.summary: This program asks you for the current temperature and, when it is below 10 degrees Celsius, advises you to wear a hat. It is the smallest possible example of a decision in code.

lines.text: input always hands back text, so float converts what you typed into a decimal number that can be compared with other numbers.
The comparison produces either True or False, and the indented block below runs only when the result is True.
The indentation is what makes this line belong to the if; type 15 and nothing is printed at all, because there is no else branch.

prompts.prompt: Modify this code to also tell you when not to wear a hat.

explanation.summary: This program asks for the current temperature and then advises whether you need a hat. It uses an if/else pair so that exactly one of the two messages is printed, no matter what number you type.

lines.text: input always hands back text, so float() converts what was typed into a decimal number that can be compared with 10. The result is stored in temp for the test on the next line.
This is the condition that decides everything: if the temperature is below 10 degrees, the indented block underneath runs.
The indentation is what ties this line to the if above it, making it the cold-weather advice.
The else branch covers every case the condition missed — here, 10 degrees or warmer — so the program always gives an answer.
This is the addition the exercise asks for, telling the reader when a hat is unnecessary rather than staying silent.

prompts.prompt: Use an elif to tell you if you need to wear sunscreen because it's too hot

explanation.summary: This program asks for a temperature and gives clothing advice, choosing between three possible messages depending on how cold or hot it is.

lines.text: input always hands back text, so float converts what the reader typed into a decimal number that can be compared with 10 and 30.
The first condition is checked first; if it is true, the rest of the chain is skipped entirely.
elif means "otherwise, check this instead," so this test only runs when the temperature was not below 10 -- that is what makes the three outcomes mutually exclusive.
The else branch catches everything left over, here the comfortable range from 10 up to 30, so the program always prints exactly one message.

examples.title: Dessert Recommendation with Nested Ifs
examples.description: Nested if loop program that recommends a dessert based on the weather and liking chocolate.
examples.prompt: Write a 12 line program with nested ifs to decide what dessert you should have based on whether it is hot outside and whether you like chocolate.

explanation.summary: This program asks two yes/no questions and combines the answers to pick a dessert. It uses one if/else nested inside another, so the four possible answer pairs each lead to their own result.

lines.text: Reads the first answer and cleans it up immediately: `.strip()` removes stray spaces around what was typed, and `.lower()` turns `Y` into `y` so the comparisons below only need to check one form.
Collects and tidies the second answer the same way, storing it in its own variable so both answers are available at once.
The outer decision splits the program into a hot-weather path and a cool-weather path.
The inner decision runs only when it is hot, so it chooses between the two hot-weather desserts. Notice the extra indentation: that is what makes this if belong inside the one above.
Each branch does nothing but store a name in the same variable, which keeps the printing in one place at the end.
This `else` pairs with the outer `if`, so it handles every case where the weather is not hot.
A second inner decision, indented under the outer `else`, covers the two cool-weather desserts.
Back at the leftmost indentation, so it runs no matter which branch was taken; whichever value `dessert` received is the one reported.

examples.title: Hello Three Times
examples.description: Using a for loop to print "Hello" three times.
examples.prompt: Write a program that says hello three times.

explanation.summary: This program prints the word "Hello" three times using a loop, so the instruction only has to be written once.

lines.text: range(3) produces the three numbers 0, 1, and 2, and the for loop runs its body once for each of them. The variable i holds the current number, even though this program never uses it.
The indentation is what puts this line inside the loop, so it runs on every pass rather than just once.

examples.title: Count from 1 to 5
examples.description: For loop that counts from 1 to 5.
examples.prompt: Write a short program that counts from 1 to 5

explanation.summary: This program prints the numbers 1 through 5, one per line, using a for loop over a range of numbers.

lines.text: range(1, 6) produces the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — the first number is included but the second is not, so you write one past where you want to stop. On each pass through the loop, the variable i holds the next number in that sequence.
The indentation is what places this line inside the loop, so it runs once for every value of i.

examples.title: Count Down from 5 to 1
examples.description: For loop with three arguments that counts down.
examples.prompt: Write a short program that counts from 5 to 1.

explanation.summary: This program counts backwards, printing the numbers 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1 on separate lines. It shows how a range can walk downwards instead of upwards.

lines.text: The three arguments to range are the start, the stop, and the step. Starting at 5 and stepping by -1 counts down, and because the stop value is never included, the sequence ends at 1 rather than 0.
The indented body runs once for each value the loop hands to i, so each countdown number appears on its own line.

examples.title: Multiplication Table with Nested Loops
examples.description: Nested for loop multiplication table program.
examples.prompt: Use nested loops to output the times table up to 10 without headings.

explanation.summary: This program prints a 10 by 10 multiplication table using one loop inside another. The outer loop picks a row, the inner loop prints every product in that row, and each number is padded so the columns line up.

lines.text: The outer loop walks through the rows, giving i the values 1 through 10; range stops just before its second argument, so 11 is needed to include 10.
For every single value of i, this inner loop runs all the way from 1 to 10, which is what produces 100 products in total.
The f-string format :3 pads each product to three characters wide so the columns stay aligned, and end=' ' replaces the usual newline with a space so the row keeps building on one line.
This empty print belongs to the outer loop, so after each finished row it emits the newline that end=' ' suppressed, moving on to the next row.

examples.title: Loop Over Musical Scale
examples.description: For loop that loops over the "letters" string.
examples.prompt: Write a program that stores the musical letters in a string and then prints them one per line.

explanation.summary: This program stores the seven musical note names in a single string and prints each letter on its own line. It shows that a for loop can walk through the characters of a string, not just numbers.

lines.text: The seven note names are held in one string. A string is a sequence of characters, so Python can step through it one character at a time.
Each pass through the loop assigns the next character of the string to the variable letter, in the order they appear.
Indented inside the loop, this runs once per character, giving one note per line.

examples.title: Feed Parrot Until Full
examples.description: While loop program for feeding a parrot.
examples.prompt: Write an 8 line program where you keep feeding the parrot seeds until it is full.
response: print(f"Parrot needs {capacity} seeds to be full.")

explanation.summary: This program asks the reader to hand the parrot seeds over and over, adding each handful to a running total, and stops as soon as the parrot has received the 10 seeds it needs.

lines.text: This is the target the loop is working towards: the number of seeds the parrot needs before it counts as full.
A running total, starting at zero because nothing has been fed yet. Counters like this must exist before the loop that updates them.
The loop repeats as long as the total is still short of the target, so the program does not need to know in advance how many handfuls it will take.
Each pass reads one handful from the keyboard and converts the text to a whole number, showing how many seeds are still outstanding so the reader can decide what to type.
The total grows by the amount just entered, and max(0, feed) quietly turns a negative entry into zero so nobody can take seeds back out of the parrot.
Reporting both this handful and the running total makes the loop's progress visible on each pass.
This line sits outside the loop, so it runs once the condition finally fails — that is, the moment the total reaches capacity.

examples.title: Count to 10 Skip Multiples of 3
examples.description: Program which counts to 10 and uses a continue to skip multiples of 3.
examples.prompt: Write a while loop that prints numbers from 1 to 10, but skips every multiple of 3.

explanation.summary: This program counts from 1 to 10 with a while loop, printing each number except the multiples of 3. It uses `continue` to jump straight back to the top of the loop when a number should be skipped.

lines.text: The counter starts at 1 because that is the first number we want to print.
The loop keeps running as long as the counter has not passed 10, so the last number considered is 10 itself.
The remainder operator `%` gives what is left over after dividing; a remainder of 0 means `i` divides evenly by 3 and should be skipped.
The counter must be advanced here, before skipping, or the loop would come back to the same multiple of 3 forever.
`continue` abandons the rest of this pass through the loop and jumps back to the `while` test, so the `print` below never runs for a multiple of 3.
This line is only reached for numbers that survived the skip test, which is exactly what we want on screen.
This is the normal increment for numbers that were printed, keeping the loop marching towards 10.

examples.title: Count Until User Says Stop
examples.description: Number counter program that will stop counting when the user says stop.
examples.prompt: Write a 9 line program that keeps counting until the user says stop.
response: s = input("Press Enter to continue or type stop: ")

explanation.summary: This program counts upward, pausing after each number to wait for the user, and keeps going until the user types "stop". It shows how an infinite loop can be ended on purpose with `break`.

lines.text: The counter starts at 1 so the first number shown is 1 rather than 0.
The condition is always true, so the loop never ends on its own; something inside the body must stop it.

lines.code: s = input("Press Enter to continue or type stop: ")
lines.text: Reading input inside the loop is what makes the user, rather than a fixed number, decide when to finish.
`strip()` removes stray spaces and `lower()` folds capital letters, so "STOP" and " Stop " are all accepted.
`break` leaves the loop immediately, which is the only exit from a `while True` like this one.
This runs only when the user did not say stop, so the count advances by one for the next pass.

examples.title: If/Else with Booleans
examples.prompt: Modify the program with a yes/no question to ask the user if they would like to use Celsius

explanation.summary: This program asks whether you want to enter the temperature in Celsius, converts from Fahrenheit when you say no, and then advises what to wear based on the result.

lines.text: The answer is cleaned up with .strip() to drop stray spaces and .lower() to ignore capitalisation, then compared to "yes"; the comparison produces True or False, so use_celsius holds a boolean rather than text.
A boolean variable can be tested directly, with no comparison needed — this reads almost like an English sentence.
input always hands back text, so float converts it into a number that can be compared and used in arithmetic.
The Fahrenheit reading is stored under its own name to keep it distinct from the Celsius value used later.
This is the standard Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula, so that both branches leave temp in the same units.
Only after the two branches have agreed on a Celsius value does the advice logic begin.
elif is only reached when the first test failed, so this check quietly means "between 10 and 30 was ruled out".
The else branch catches every temperature that neither earlier test claimed, guaranteeing exactly one message is printed.

examples.title: While Loops
examples.prompt: Parrot needs 10 seeds to be full.

explanation.summary: This loop keeps asking for seeds until the parrot has been fed at least as many as its capacity, adding each amount to a running total. It shows the shape of a while loop: a condition that is checked before every pass, and a body that changes the values in that condition so the loop can eventually end.

lines.text: The condition is tested before each pass, so the loop keeps going only while the total fed so far is still below what the parrot needs. Because `fed` grows inside the body, the loop is guaranteed to finish.
The prompt is rebuilt each pass so it can show `capacity-fed`, the seeds still needed, and `int(...)` turns the typed text into a whole number you can do arithmetic with.
`max(0, feed)` treats any negative entry as zero, so a mischievous reader cannot undo progress and trap the loop forever.
Reporting both the single helping and the running total lets you watch the loop variable climb toward the capacity on every pass.

fed = 0
capacity = 10

# Run the feeding loop printed in the book.
exec(open("while_loops.py").read())

print("The parrot is full!")

examples.title: Counting Down and For Loop Syntax
examples.prompt: Write a short rocket program that counts from 5 to 1.

explanation.summary: This program counts backwards from 5 down to 1, pausing one second between each number, then announces a rocket blastoff.

lines.text: The time module comes with Python and provides tools for working with clocks and delays; importing it makes those tools available in this file.
The three arguments to range are the start, the stop, and the step: begin at 5, count by -1, and halt before reaching 0, so i takes the values 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
Pausing the program for one second turns a wall of instant output into a countdown the reader can actually watch tick by.
Because this line sits outside the loop's indentation, it runs once after the countdown finishes rather than on every pass.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Data Structures
chapters.goal: Learn the core Python data structures by building applications that demonstrate these concepts and learning from the illustrated explanations of these important concepts.

examples.title: Accessing and Modifying Lists
examples.prompt: Modify the list to include a Portuguese item that would be easy to buy in a grocery store. Use changing, adding, removing, then accessing at the end.
response: shopping_list[4] = "chouriço"  # Replace snacks with Portuguese sausage
shopping_list.append("pastéis de nata")  # Portuguese custard tarts

explanation.summary: This program builds a party shopping list, then edits it three ways \at the end, and finally reads items back out by position.

lines.text: A list holds several values in one variable, in the order you write them. Square brackets create the list, and commas separate the items.

lines.code: shopping_list[4] = "chouriço"  # Replace snacks with Portuguese sausage
lines.text: Lists are mutable, so you can overwrite a single slot by assigning to its index. Counting starts at 0, so index 4 is the fifth item, "snacks".

lines.code: shopping_list.append("pastéis de nata")  # Portuguese custard tarts
lines.text: The append method adds one new item to the end of the list, making the list longer by one.
The remove method deletes an item by its value rather than its position, so you do not have to know where "balloons" sits.
A for loop visits each item in the list in turn, storing the current one in the variable item.
Passing two arguments to print puts a space between them, which gives each line a dash and then the item.
Index 0 is always the first item. The \n inside the f-string prints a blank line first, which separates the summary from the list above.
A negative index counts backwards from the end, so -1 is the last item no matter how long the list has become.

examples.title: Iterating Over a List
examples.prompt: Write an 7 line roll call program that goes through a fixed list of students, asks if they are present, and prints the list of absentees.

explanation.summary: This program walks through a fixed list of student names, asks whether each one is present, and collects the names of everyone who was not marked present into a second list that it prints at the end.

lines.text: A list holds several values in order under one name, so the whole roll can be stored in a single variable.
An empty list is created before the loop begins so there is somewhere to accumulate names as they are discovered.
The for loop hands the body one name at a time, which saves writing the same question five times over.
The f-string drops the current name straight into the question, and .lower() folds the reply to lowercase so "Yes" and "YES" are treated the same as "yes".
Anything other than "yes" counts as absent, which means a blank line or a typo is treated as a no rather than silently passing.
append adds the name to the end of the absentees list, growing it as the loop runs.
Printing after the loop finishes gives one summary of the whole roll call instead of a message per student.

examples.title: Sorting Lists
examples.prompt: Create a program that creates a list of fish types with some duplicates and sorts them alphabetically

explanation.summary: This program stores eight fish names in a list, including a repeated entry, and rearranges them into alphabetical order before printing them.

lines.text: A list holds items in the order you write them, and it happily accepts duplicates, so "Salmon" appears twice here.
The sort method reorders the list in place, alphabetically for strings, rather than returning a new list. Notice that both copies of "Salmon" survive the sort and end up next to each other.
Printing the list itself shows the square brackets and quotes, which confirms the new order at a glance.

examples.title: Tuples
examples.prompt: Using only tuples, describe a car with different attributes.

explanation.summary: This program packs nine facts about a car into a single tuple and then reads a few of them back out by position. A tuple is an ordered, fixed collection of values that cannot be changed after it is created.

lines.text: The parentheses open a tuple that will hold every attribute of one car; spreading it over several lines keeps it readable and lets each value carry a comment.
The first value is the make, and because tuples keep their order, "Toyota" will stay at position 0 for the life of this tuple.
A tuple can mix types freely, so a whole number sits happily alongside the text values.
The last item takes no trailing comma, and the closing parenthesis on the next line finishes the tuple.
Indexing starts at 0, so these three lookups pull the make, model, and year out to build a headline for the car.
Here is the weakness of describing something with a bare tuple: you must remember that 5 means colour and 7 means fuel type, which is why dictionaries later in this chapter are often a better fit.

examples.title: Unpacking Tuples
examples.prompt: Write a program that uses tuple unpacking for Sam's winter gear. Unpack his clothes into three categories: a hat, outerwear, and shoes.
response: # Unpack the tuple into three categories

explanation.summary: This program stores three items of winter clothing in a tuple, then uses tuple unpacking to give each item its own descriptive name before printing them.

lines.text: A tuple holds the three pieces of gear in a fixed order. The order matters here, because unpacking relies on it.

Tuple unpacking assigns the three values to three variables in one step, matching them up by position. The number of names on the left must equal the number of items in the tuple, or Python raises an error.
A heading for the output. The f prefix is harmless but unnecessary here, since there are no placeholders to fill in.
An f-string inserts the value of hat where the braces appear, which is why unpacking into meaningful names pays off.

examples.title: Creating Dictionaries
examples.prompt: Create a dictionary for a fantasy world item shop containing a sword, a spell, and a potion, along with their price.

explanation.summary: This builds a dictionary that maps the name of each shop item to its price in gold. A dictionary stores pairs of keys and values, so you can look up a price by the item's name instead of by a numeric position.

lines.text: Curly braces begin a dictionary literal, and the name `shop` will refer to the finished collection.
The text before the colon is the key and the number after it is the value, so `shop["sword"]` will give back 150.
The final pair needs no trailing comma, and the closing brace on the next line ends the dictionary.

examples.title: Storing Lists in Dictionaries
examples.prompt: Create a dictionary for student classes at a magic academy. Create lists of classes for Sally and four other students.

explanation.summary: This program builds a dictionary where each key is a student's name and each value is a list of the classes that student takes, then prints one line per student. It shows that a dictionary value can be a whole list, not just a single number or string.

lines.text: This opens the dictionary literal. Spreading it over several lines keeps each student on their own line and is easier to read than one long line.
The key is the student's name and the value is a list of four class names, so a single lookup gives you Sally's entire schedule.
The last entry before the closing brace needs no trailing comma, though Python would accept one.
The items() method hands back each key and value together, so student holds the name and classes holds that student's list on every pass through the loop.
join() glues the list of class names into one string separated by commas, which reads far better than printing the raw list with its brackets and quotes.

examples.title: Try/Except
examples.prompt: Ask for user input to share cupcakes among llamas. Handle errors accordingly
response: cupcakes = int(input("How many cupcakes do you have? "))
llamas = int(input("How many llamas are sharing the cupcakes? "))
print("Error: Please enter valid whole numbers for cupcakes and llamas.")
print("Error: You can't share cupcakes among zero llamas!")

explanation.summary: This program asks how many cupcakes and how many llamas there are, then divides to see how many cupcakes each llama gets. The try/except blocks catch two things that can go wrong: text that isn't a number, and dividing by zero llamas.

lines.text: Everything indented under `try:` is code that might fail. If any line in the block raises an error, Python stops running the block and looks for a matching `except` below.

lines.code: cupcakes = int(input("How many cupcakes do you have? "))
lines.text: `input` always hands back text, so `int` converts it to a whole number. If the reader types something like "twelve", `int` raises a ValueError here.
The `/` operator divides and gives a decimal result. If `llamas` is 0, this raises a ZeroDivisionError instead of producing a number.
The `:.2f` inside the f-string rounds the result to two decimal places, so you see 4.00 rather than a long string of digits.
This block runs only when a conversion to `int` failed, and it lets the program finish with a friendly message rather than crashing.
A second `except` handles a different kind of error, so each problem gets its own explanation of what went wrong.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Functions
chapters.goal: Understand how to modularize applications using functions and lambdas to create more maintainable code.

examples.title: Single-Argument Functions
examples.prompt: Write a function to help Beepo the robot waiter roll up to the correct table and greet. The function should take one argument for the table number. Call the function three times.
response: """Beepo the robot waiter greets at the specified table."""
print(f"Beep boop! Rolling up to table {table_number}...")
print(f"Welcome to table {table_number}! How can I assist you today?")

explanation.summary: This program defines a function that greets diners at a numbered table, then calls it three times with different table numbers. It shows how one block of code can be reused with different input.

lines.text: The `def` keyword defines a new function named `beepo_greet`, and `table_number` is its parameter -- a placeholder that receives whatever value the caller supplies.

lines.code: """Beepo the robot waiter greets at the specified table."""
lines.text: A string on the first line of a function is a docstring, the standard way to record what the function is for so tools and other readers can find it.

lines.code: print(f"Beep boop! Rolling up to table {table_number}...")
lines.text: The `f` before the quotes makes this an f-string, so `{table_number}` is replaced by the value passed in rather than printed literally.

lines.code: print(f"Welcome to table {table_number}! How can I assist you today?")
lines.text: Both print statements are indented, which is how Python knows they belong to the function body and only run when the function is called.
Calling the function runs its body with `table_number` set to 1; without a call like this, the definition alone would produce no output.
The same function handles a different table simply by passing a different argument, which is the whole point of a parameter.
A third call proves the function is reusable: two lines of logic serve every table in the restaurant.

examples.title: Multi-Argument Functions
examples.prompt: Create a function to help Beepo the robot waiter to deliver food to a table. The function should take two arguments: a food list and table number. Call the function twice.
response: """Helps Beepo the robot waiter deliver food to a table."""

explanation.summary: This program defines a function that takes two pieces of information — a list of food items and a table number — and prints a delivery report for Beepo the robot waiter. The function is then called twice with different orders, showing how one definition can serve many situations.

lines.text: Defines a function with two parameters, separated by a comma. When the function is called, the first value given becomes `food_list` and the second becomes `table_number`.

lines.code: """Helps Beepo the robot waiter deliver food to a table."""
lines.text: A docstring: a short description placed as the first line inside a function so that anyone reading the code knows its purpose.
An f-string drops the value of `table_number` straight into the sentence, so the heading names the correct table each time.
Because `food_list` is a list, a loop can walk through it one item at a time, no matter how many items the order contains.
The two leading spaces and the dash format each item as an indented bullet under the heading.
The `\n` adds an extra blank line at the end, which keeps the two deliveries visually separate in the output.
Calls the function with a list of three foods and table 5. The arguments are matched to the parameters by position, so order matters.
A second call with entirely different values proves the point of functions: the logic is written once and reused.

examples.title: Function Returns
examples.prompt: Create a function to help Beepo the robot waiter take payment from a numbered table according to the items ordered (everything costs $2). Call the function three times to collect money, put it in the cash register, and print the total.
response: """Collects payment from a table based on items ordered ($2 each)"""

explanation.summary: This program defines a function that works out what a table owes ($2 per item), prints the bill, and hands the amount back to the caller. The three returned amounts are added into a running cash register total.

lines.text: The function takes two pieces of information: which table is paying, and the list of things they ordered.

lines.code: """Collects payment from a table based on items ordered ($2 each)"""
lines.text: A docstring is a short description placed as the first line inside a function, so anyone reading or using it knows its purpose.
len() counts how many items are in the list, and multiplying by 2 gives the bill in dollars.
Beepo announces the bill out loud, showing the working so the customer can check it.
return sends the value back to whoever called the function, so the amount can be used in a calculation rather than just printed.
The register starts empty; this variable will accumulate every payment collected.
The function runs, and the number it returns is added straight into the register with +=. This is why returning a value is more useful than only printing one.
The same function handles a four-item order without any changes, which is the whole point of writing it once.
The \n inserts a blank line before the total, separating the summary from the individual bills above.

examples.title: Playing High Card
examples.prompt: Use this generator to play one hand of high card.
response: deck = [(f'{rank} of {suit}', value) for suit in suits for value, rank in enumerate(ranks)]

explanation.summary: This program builds a shuffled 52-card deck inside a generator function, deals one card to the player and one to the computer, and compares their ranks to declare a winner. It shows how a generator can hand out values one at a time with `next()`.

lines.text: Brings in the random module so the deck can be shuffled into an unpredictable order.
Defines a generator function: because its body contains `yield`, calling it does not run the code immediately but returns an object you can pull cards from one at a time.
The four suits, which supply the second half of each card's name.
The thirteen ranks listed from lowest to highest, so their positions in the list double as their comparison values.

lines.code: deck = [(f'{rank} of {suit}', value) for suit in suits for value, rank in enumerate(ranks)]
lines.text: A nested list comprehension pairs every rank with every suit, producing 52 tuples of (name, value); `enumerate` supplies the value, giving '2' a 0 and 'Ace' a 12.
Rearranges the list in place so the cards come out in a random order instead of suit by suit.
Walks the shuffled deck from the top.
Hands one card back to the caller and pauses here; the next request resumes the loop at the following card.
Creates the generator object. Nothing has been shuffled yet — the function body only starts running when the first card is requested.
Draws two cards with `next()` and unpacks each (name, value) tuple into its own pair of variables in one statement.
Shows both hands so the reader can see what was dealt before the verdict.
Starts a chained conditional expression that picks one of three strings; because the comparison uses the numeric value, 'King' correctly beats '10'.
The second branch handles the computer's higher card, and its own `else` below covers the remaining case.
The final fallback, reached when both cards share the same rank in different suits.

examples.title: Filter Function
examples.prompt: Create a list of goats and use filter to get the calmest ones.

explanation.summary: This program stores a herd of goats as a list of dictionaries, then uses filter with a lambda to pick out only the goats whose calm level is 7 or higher and prints them.

lines.text: Starts a list where each item will be a dictionary describing one goat, a common way to hold several pieces of information about many things.
Each dictionary pairs the key "name" with a goat's name and "calm_level" with a number, so both facts travel together as one item.
filter runs the little lambda function on every goat and keeps only those for which it returns True; list() turns the result into a real list you can loop over more than once.
The \n prints a blank line first, which separates the heading from anything above it in the terminal.
Walks through the filtered list one goat at a time so each survivor can be printed.
An f-string pulls both values out of the dictionary by key; note the single quotes inside, since the f-string itself already uses double quotes.

examples.title: Reduce Function
examples.prompt: Use reduce to calculate how many eggs a list of chickens laid in total. Then calculate how many muffins can be made from those eggs (1 egg per 6 muffins)
response: total_eggs = reduce(lambda total, chicken: total + chicken["eggs_laid"], chickens, 0)

explanation.summary: This program adds up the eggs laid by a list of chickens using reduce, then works out how many muffins that many eggs can produce. It shows how reduce collapses a whole list down into a single value.

lines.text: Unlike map and filter, reduce is not built in; it lives in the functools module and has to be imported before you can use it.
Starts a list of dictionaries, where each dictionary is one chicken with a name and an egg count.
Each entry pairs the key "name" with a string and the key "eggs_laid" with a number, so the reduce below can look up "eggs_laid" on every chicken.

lines.code: total_eggs = reduce(lambda total, chicken: total + chicken["eggs_laid"], chickens, 0)
lines.text: reduce walks the list one chicken at a time, carrying a running total. The lambda receives that total and the current chicken and returns the new total; the final 0 is the starting value, so the result is 25.
Turns the egg count into muffins at the stated rate of six muffins per egg.
An f-string drops the value of the variable straight into the message inside the braces.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Object-Oriented Programming
chapters.goal: Learn object-oriented programming techniques that provide encapsulation and abstraction for building more complex applications.

examples.title: Classes and Attributes
examples.prompt: Create a robot pet class with the attributes name, battery, and mood. Then create three pets and print their attributes.

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet class that stores a name, battery level, and mood, then builds three separate pets from that one blueprint and prints each one's details.

lines.text: This begins the blueprint for a robot pet. A class does not hold data itself; it describes what every pet made from it will look like.
The __init__ method runs automatically each time a new pet is created, and it receives the starting values for that pet. The first parameter, self, refers to the particular pet being built.
Storing the name on self attaches it to this individual pet, so it survives after __init__ finishes.
Each pet gets its own battery level, independent of the other pets.
The mood is the third attribute, completing the set of data every pet carries.
Calling the class like a function creates one pet object; the three arguments land in the name, battery, and mood parameters of __init__.
A second pet from the same class shows that one blueprint can produce many objects, each with its own values.
Dot notation reads an attribute back out of an object, and the f-string drops those values straight into the message.

examples.title: Methods
examples.prompt: Add a method that checks if the pet has enough energy for a walk with a duration you can set and check the animals to see if they can do a 30 minute walk.
response: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
# Check if pets can do a 30 minute walk

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet class with a method that decides whether a pet has enough battery for a walk of a given length, then tests three pets against a 30-minute walk.

lines.text: The initializer runs automatically whenever a new RobotPet is created, receiving the values that describe that particular pet.
Storing the argument on self keeps the name attached to this specific pet object rather than losing it when __init__ ends.
A method is a function that lives inside the class; self refers to the pet it is called on, and duration is supplied by the caller.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: This docstring documents what the method expects and what it answers, so anyone reading the class later knows duration is in minutes.
The rule of the program: each minute of walking costs two units of battery.
A comparison evaluates to True or False, so the method hands that answer straight back to the caller.
Calling the class like a function creates an object, passing the three values along to __init__.
Dot notation reads the attributes back out of the object inside an f-string.
The \n escape prints a blank line first, separating the pet list from the walk results.
Calling the method on pet1 passes that pet as self automatically, so 30 fills in duration; Rover's 85 battery clears the 60 required.
Beep has only 45 battery, so the same method returns False, showing that each object carries its own data.

examples.title: Encapsulation
examples.prompt: Use encapsulation to protect the battery attribute and ensure it doesn't go above 100 or below 0
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
"""Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet class that guards its battery level with a property, so any value assigned is clamped into the range 0 to 100. Three pets are created and their details printed.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Even inside the constructor, this assignment goes through the property setter rather than storing the value directly, so a bad starting battery is corrected right away.
The @property decorator turns the method below into a read-only attribute: readers write pet.battery, not pet.battery().
This getter hands back the internally stored value. The leading underscore in _battery signals that outside code should leave it alone and use the property instead.
This decorator registers the next method as the code that runs whenever something assigns to .battery, which is where the validation lives.
The setter receives the value being assigned and decides what actually gets stored.
Anything negative is treated as an empty battery rather than being rejected with an error.
Anything above full is capped, so the battery can never claim more charge than it holds.
A value already inside the valid range is stored unchanged.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring documents what the method expects and returns; help(RobotPet.can_walk) will show this text.
Naming the calculation makes the rule visible, so the walking cost can be tuned in one place.
The comparison itself is either True or False, so it can be returned directly without an if statement.
Creating an instance runs __init__, which routes the battery value through the validating setter.
Reading pet1.battery quietly calls the getter, which is the point of encapsulation: the protection is invisible at the point of use.

examples.title: Encapsulation
examples.prompt: Test walk and charge methods on Rover
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
"""Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
# Test walk and charge methods on Rover
print(f"{pet1.name} doesn't have enough battery to walk {duration} minutes.")
print(f"{pet1.name} doesn't have enough battery to walk {duration} minutes.")

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet class whose battery level is guarded by a property setter that keeps the value between 0 and 100, then walks and charges a pet named Rover to show the guard at work.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery here does not create a plain attribute; because a property named battery exists, Python routes this through the setter, so even the starting value gets validated.
The @property decorator turns the method below into a read-only-looking attribute, so callers write pet.battery instead of pet.battery().
The real value lives in _battery, and the leading underscore signals that outside code should leave it alone and go through the property instead.
This registers the next method as the code that runs whenever anything assigns to .battery, which is the heart of encapsulation: one gatekeeper for every write.
A walk that drains more energy than remains would push the battery negative, so the setter clamps it.
Charging past a full battery is meaningless, so anything above 100 is capped at 100.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring documents what the method promises, and tools such as help() display it.
Naming the calculation makes the cost rule explicit and keeps can_walk and walk consistent about what a minute costs.
The -= reads the property and then assigns back through the setter, so the clamping rules apply automatically.
Creating an instance runs __init__, giving Rover his own name, battery, and mood.
Asking before acting is the point of can_walk: a ten-minute walk costs 20%, which Rover can afford.
A fifty-minute walk would cost 100%, more than Rover has left, so this run takes the else branch and demonstrates the guard.
Charging pushes the total above 100, letting the setter's upper cap show itself in the printed result.

examples.title: Inheritance
examples.prompt: Add robot pet subclasses for a cat, bird, and dog. Then create one of each type. Finally, call each animal’s method.
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation

explanation.summary: This program defines a general RobotPet class and then three specialised versions of it — a cat, a bird, and a dog — each adding its own sound method. One of each is created and asked to speak.

lines.text: The base class holds everything the three pets have in common, so that shared code is written once.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery does not store the value directly; it runs the setter below, so an out-of-range battery is corrected on the way in.
The @property decorator turns the method beneath it into an attribute you read as pet.battery, with no parentheses.
The real value lives in the underscore-prefixed _battery, and the property hands it out on request.
This marks the next method as the code to run whenever something assigns to battery.
Negative charges are meaningless, so anything below zero is clamped up to zero.
Likewise a battery cannot exceed full, so anything above 100 is clamped down.
Putting RobotPet in parentheses means RobotCat inherits its __init__ and its battery property without repeating a line of them.
This is the cat's own addition — a method that exists only on RobotCat, not on the base class or its siblings.
The subclass can read self.name even though the base class set it, because an inherited attribute belongs to the object itself.
A second subclass built from the same base, showing that one parent can have many children.
The third subclass follows the identical pattern, differing only in the sound it makes.
No __init__ is written in RobotCat, so Python falls back to the one it inherited from RobotPet.
Each object is asked for its own specialised behaviour, which is the payoff of writing separate subclasses.

examples.title: Calling Super Methods
examples.prompt: The talents should use the battery. Put this logic in the base class instead of performing a generic trick.
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
return f"{self.name} has no battery left and cannot perform!"
return f"{self.name} is low on battery and can barely perform..."
return f"{self.name} gracefully balances on two legs! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"
return f"{self.name} mimics a beautiful melody! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"
return f"{self.name} catches a frisbee in mid-air! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"

explanation.summary: Three kinds of robot pet share one battery check that lives in the base class, and each subclass calls `super().show_talent()` first to see whether the battery is too low before describing its own trick.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to `self.battery` in the constructor runs the property setter below, so a value out of range is clamped before it is ever stored.
The `@property` decorator turns the `battery` method into an attribute read, so `pet.battery` returns the stored value without any parentheses.
The matching setter runs every time something assigns to `battery`, which is where the validation rule is enforced.
A negative charge makes no sense, so it is clamped to empty rather than being rejected.
Anything over a full charge is capped at 100 percent.
The base class owns only the shared part of the behaviour: deciding whether the battery permits a performance at all.
Returning `None` is the base class's way of saying "the battery is fine, carry on", which is the signal each subclass tests for.
`super()` reaches the version of `show_talent` defined in `RobotPet`, so the battery rules are written once and reused by every subclass.
If the parent returned a message, the battery is too low and that message is passed straight back instead of the trick.

lines.code: return f"{self.name} gracefully balances on two legs! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"
lines.text: Only when the parent gave the all-clear does the subclass add its own unique behaviour.
Putting different subclasses in one list works because they all understand `show_talent`, which is the heart of polymorphism.
The same call produces a different result for each pet, and Python picks the right version at runtime.

examples.title: Composition
examples.prompt: Create a RobotPetShelter class that stores robot pet objects in a list that is encapsulated. Add methods to add a pet, show all pets, and find a pet by name. Then create some pets.

explanation.summary: This program builds a RobotPetShelter that keeps its collection of robot pets in a private list, and gives the outside world three safe ways to work with that list: add a pet, print them all, and search for one by name. It is an example of composition — a shelter is not a kind of pet, it is an object made up of other objects.

lines.text: The double underscore makes the list private to the shelter, so nothing outside the class can add, remove, or reorder pets without going through the shelter's own methods.
This is the only doorway into the private list, and it accepts any object that behaves like a robot pet.
An empty list is falsy in Python, so this is the idiomatic way to handle the "nothing here yet" case before trying to build a report.
Joining with a newline turns the many pet descriptions into one multi-line string, which the caller can print in a single go.
type(pet).__name__ pulls out the class name of each object, so the report shows whether a pet is a RobotCat, RobotBird, or RobotDog without the shelter needing to know in advance.
This generator expression feeds one formatted line per pet into join, rather than building an intermediate list.
Lowercasing both sides makes the search case-insensitive, so "rex" and "Rex" find the same pet.
Returning None when nothing matches is the standard Python signal for "not found", and it lets the caller test the result with a simple if.
The three pets come from the subclasses written earlier in the chapter; the shelter never needs to know which subclass it is holding.
The shelter starts out empty because its constructor takes no arguments and creates a fresh list.
Adding objects one at a time is what composition looks like in practice: the shelter now contains the pets rather than inheriting from them.
The search hands back the actual RobotDog object, not a copy, so any method on that object can be called next.
Guarding the call protects against the None case; calling a method on None would crash the program.
Because the returned object is a real RobotDog, its own version of show_talent runs — polymorphism working through the shelter.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Unit Tests
chapters.goal: AI is a great assistant for unit testing. Learn how to apply AI to automatically write unit tests and assertions of your code.

examples.title: Assert
examples.prompt: Create a RobotPet class and a method that checks if the pet has enough battery to go on a walk.
response: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""

explanation.summary: This defines a RobotPet class that stores a name, a battery level, and a mood, plus a can_walk method that decides whether the pet has enough battery for a walk of a given length. Two pets are then created so the method has something to be tested against.

lines.text: The initializer runs whenever a new RobotPet is created and receives the three values that describe the pet.
Storing the battery level on the object is what later lets can_walk compare it against the energy a walk needs.
This is the behaviour worth testing: it takes a walk length and answers a yes-or-no question about it.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring records the rule the method implements, including the unit of duration, so a reader never has to guess whether it means minutes or hours.
The cost rule is that each minute of walking drains two units of battery.
The comparison produces True or False directly, which is exactly the kind of clear-cut result an assertion can check.
Rover has a healthy battery, so it will serve as the example that should be allowed to walk.
Beep starts with much less charge, giving you a second case that fails for longer walks.

examples.title: Assert
examples.prompt: Add two unit tests using assert to check if the pets can walk
response: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
assert rover.can_walk(30) == True, "Rover should be able to walk for 30 minutes"
assert beep.can_walk(30) == False, "Beep should not be able to walk for 30 minutes"

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet class with a can_walk method that compares the pet's battery level against the energy a walk would need, then checks the method's behaviour with two assert statements. If both checks hold, the program prints a success message.

lines.text: The constructor runs whenever a new RobotPet is created and receives the three values that describe the pet.
Stores the battery level on the object so that can_walk can consult it later.
Defines the behaviour under test: given a walk length in minutes, decide whether this pet has the energy for it.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring records the method's contract in the code itself, so anyone reading or testing it knows what the units are.
Fixes the rule that every minute of walking costs two units of battery, giving the test a predictable number to work with.
Returns True or False by comparing the stored battery to the cost, which is exactly the value the asserts examine.
Creates a well-charged pet that should pass the walk check, setting up the positive test case.

"""Runs the printed test file.

The book replaces each setUp method with an ellipsis, which Python cannot
parse. This runner drops those placeholder lines, then supplies the setUp
methods the chapter described so the tests can execute unchanged.
"""

import os
import unittest

from pet_talents import RobotPet, RobotCat, RobotBird, RobotDog

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
TARGET = "implementing_a_new_feature_and_testing_it.py"
ME = os.path.basename(__file__)


def find_source():
    direct = os.path.join(HERE, TARGET)
    if os.path.exists(direct):
        return direct
    for name in sorted(os.listdir(HERE)):
        if not name.endswith(".py") or name in (ME, "pet_talents.py"):
            continue
        path = os.path.join(HERE, name)
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            if "class TestRobotPet" in handle.read():
                return path
    raise SystemExit("Could not find the book's test file.")


with open(find_source(), encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    source = handle.read()

cleaned = "\n".join(
    line for line in source.splitlines() if line.strip() != "\u2026"
)

namespace = {"__name__": "book_tests"}
exec(compile(cleaned, "book_tests", "exec"), namespace)

SETUPS = [
    ("TestRobotPet", "pet", lambda: RobotPet("Robo")),
    ("TestRobotCat", "cat", lambda: RobotCat("Whiskers")),
    ("TestRobotBird", "bird", lambda: RobotBird("Tweety")),
    ("TestRobotDog", "dog", lambda: RobotDog("Rex")),
]


def make_setup(attribute, factory):
    def setUp(self):
        setattr(self, attribute, factory())

    return setUp


loader = unittest.TestLoader()
suite = unittest.TestSuite()
for class_name, attribute, factory in SETUPS:
    test_class = namespace[class_name]
    test_class.setUp = make_setup(attribute, factory)
    suite.addTests(loader.loadTestsFromTestCase(test_class))

unittest.TextTestRunner(verbosity=2).run(suite)

"""Runs and tests the speak() code from exercise py-7-12.

The printed listing uses the placeholder "..." for the parts of RobotPet that
were written in earlier exercises, so the file cannot be imported as it is.
This helper reads the listing, puts a real body in place of the placeholder,
and gives RobotPet the __init__ that the earlier exercises defined.
"""

import unittest
from pathlib import Path

LISTING = Path(__file__).with_name("implementing_a_new_feature_and_testing_it.py")

source = LISTING.read_text(encoding="utf-8").replace("\u2026", "pass")
classes = {}
exec(compile(source, LISTING.name, "exec"), classes)

RobotPet = classes["RobotPet"]
RobotCat = classes["RobotCat"]
RobotBird = classes["RobotBird"]
RobotDog = classes["RobotDog"]


def pet_init(self, name, mood="neutral", battery=100):
    self.name = name
    self.mood = mood
    self.battery = battery


RobotPet.__init__ = pet_init


class TestSpeak(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_low_battery_beats_mood(self):
        pet = RobotDog("Rex", mood="excited", battery=12)
        self.assertEqual(pet.speak(), "Rex says: 'Woof... need... charge...'")

    def test_full_battery_message(self):
        pet = RobotCat("Mia")
        self.assertEqual(pet.speak(), "Mia says: 'Purrr... fully charged!'")

    def test_sad_mood_message(self):
        pet = RobotBird("Kiwi", mood="sad", battery=80)
        self.assertEqual(pet.speak(), "Kiwi says: 'Tweet... *quiet chirp*'")

    def test_unknown_mood_uses_fallback(self):
        pet = RobotDog("Rex", mood="curious", battery=55)
        self.assertEqual(pet.speak(), "Rex says: 'Woof.'")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    pets = [
        RobotCat("Mia", "excited", 70),
        RobotBird("Kiwi", "sad", 80),
        RobotDog("Rex", "happy", 25),
    ]
    for pet in pets:
        print(pet.speak())
        print(pet.show_talent())
    print()
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)
